title: Open ranges on a toy graph
starter:
type node =
  | Range of string * int      (* a named loop counter and its bound *)
  | Const of int
  | Add of node * node
  | Store of node * node        (* offset, value *)
  | End of node * node          (* effect, range: closes that range *)

(* The names of the ranges [n] depends on that no End has closed, sorted, no duplicates. *)
let rec opens (n : node) : string list =
  []

tests.expr: let i = Range ("i", 4) in opens (Add (i, Const 1))
let i = Range ("i", 4) in opens (End (Store (i, i), i))
let i = Range ("i", 2) and j = Range ("j", 3) in opens (Store (Add (i, j), Const 0))
let i = Range ("i", 2) and j = Range ("j", 3) in opens (End (Store (Add (i, j), Const 0), j))
let i = Range ("i", 2) and j = Range ("j", 3) in opens (End (End (Store (Add (i, j), Const 0), j), i))
let j = Range ("j", 3) and i = Range ("i", 2) in opens (Add (j, Add (i, j)))
let k = Range ("k", 1) in opens (Add (Add (k, k), Add (k, Const 2)))

hints: A Range is open in itself. A Const has nothing open. Everything else takes the union of its children.
End (e, r) is the one exception: the opens of e, minus r's name.
Keep the result sorted and deduplicated, for example with `List.sort_uniq compare` on the combined lists.
explain: Open ranges are a union over sources, with Range adding its own name and End removing the range it closes. `List.sort_uniq compare` keeps the result canonical. The real compiler memoizes this per node, because shared subgraphs would otherwise be walked many times.
